# parity-fuzz --mode cond baseline: normalized signatures of KNOWN gaps.
# A divergence whose signature is here is allowed; a NEW one fails CI.
# Regenerate: parity-fuzz --mode cond --count N --verify 3  (copy NEW-signature lines).
#
# Covers the `test` / `[` builtin: unary flags, the three-argument binary-
# operator form, `-a`/`-o` connectives, `!`, and parenthesised groups. Both
# spellings are generated — one builtin under two funcids (BIN_TEST=20 /
# BIN_BRACKET=21, c:Src/builtin.c:7231-7247). stderr is folded into stdout
# because the diagnostics are as much the contract as the status, and the
# status alone cannot tell 1 (false) from 2 (error).
#
# EMPTY — no known gaps. Any divergence is a regression.
#
# History, kept because it explains the shape of the fix rather than the
# absence of entries. This file used to carry 68 signatures, all one gap: the
# literal string `-a` (or `-n`) used as an OPERAND next to a connective, where
# which token is the operator is genuinely ambiguous —
#
#     test -e /dev/null -a -a  → zsh 0 (the SECOND `-a` is the connective, the
#                                       third is a non-empty string), zshrs 2
#     test -a -a -a            → zsh 0,  zshrs 1
#     test '' -a -a            → zsh 1,  zshrs error
#     test ! -a                → zsh 1,  zshrs error
#     test -a a                → zsh "too many arguments" rc=2, zshrs 0
#
# C resolves these for free because it never scans for a connective: bin_test
# does only the XSI argument-count fixups and then hands the list to the real
# grammar (c:7276-7280 `condlex = testlex; testlex(); parse_cond()`), which
# consumes tokens in order — so position, not spelling, decides what is an
# operator. par_cond_2 (c:Src/parse.c:2478-2515) supplies the POSIX rules by
# ARGUMENT COUNT: n_testargs == 1 makes `[ foo ]` into `[ -n foo ]`, and
# n_testargs > 2 treats the SECOND argument as binary only when it really is
# one (`=`, `<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`, `-<condnum>`), otherwise falling through.
#
# zshrs could not reach any of that: bin_test was an ad-hoc argument-count
# parser, `testlex` was DEAD CODE (nothing referenced it) and parse.rs's
# par_cond_2 hardcodes `let n_testargs: i32 = 0`, disabling the POSIX-test rule
# set it ports. The entries were retired by doing what this file said the fix
# had to be — wiring `testlex` + `par_cond` / `par_cond_1` / `par_cond_2` /
# par_cond_double / par_cond_triple / par_cond_multi with a real `n_testargs`
# (builtin.rs, `TestParse`), NOT by adding more argument-count branches or more
# connective-scanning, which is exactly what cannot express these.
#
# Verified at 6000 cases against BOTH oracles at 0 divergences:
# /opt/homebrew/bin/zsh (zsh-5.9.2-0-gddee3e7) and /bin/zsh (zsh-5.9-0-g73d3173).
#
# NOTE on the vocabulary: `<` and `>` are NOT generated even though c:2502-2503
# lists them as three-argument binary operators. They never reach the builtin —
# the shell lexes them as redirections first, so `test b > a` runs `test b` and
# CREATES a file `a` in the harness's cwd; an earlier cut of this mode dropped
# one into the repo root. Quoting does not help: the oracle rejects
# `test a '<' b` with "condition expected: <", so there is nothing to compare.
# `[[ a < b ]]` is where those operators are reachable, and that is the `match`
# mode's surface.
